turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not aware of any misfortunes of his, beyond those which are common to the gentry. He has the advantage of youth and person over myself, and in many other respects is my superior, but this is no merit of his.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am not surprised by your ignorance of Mr Wickham's conduct, for I know how little you must see of the world beyond the narrow circle of your mother's acquaintances. But I did not invite you to be my apologist. I am not to be accused of concealing my actions. I have been most open in my declarations.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your actions are open, but your words are often guarded. I know you think little of me, but I will not be used as your apologist.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I have indeed thought little of you, Miss Bennet, but your judgment of me is no less severe. Our misunderstandings are mutual, and I must now leave you to your thoughts.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your misunderstandings of me are mutual, sir. I will think on this as you suggest, but I cannot pretend to welcome such reflections.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am aware of your estimation of me, Miss Bennet, and it is not a subject I wish to prolong. Yet, I cannot help but express my regret at the misunderstanding between us.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I understand your regret, sir, but it is not in my nature to dismiss such serious matters lightly.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that my feelings for you are not easily dismissed or altered by the opinions of others or even my own judgments. Yet, I respect your need for time and reflection.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not surprised by your confession, sir, but I must confess that your past actions have left me with much to consider and little reason to feel otherwise than I do now.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I understand the depth of your feelings towards me, and I do not seek to dismiss them lightly. My actions have been the cause of much of the discord between us, and I must live with the consequences of my past.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your confession does not alter the fact that your actions have hurt those I care about deeply. I cannot overlook this, nor can I pretend it does not affect how I feel towards you.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am aware of the pain I have caused, Elizabeth, and I do not expect to be forgiven easily. However, I hope that as time passes, you may see the man I am trying to become.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I see your sincerity, Mr. Darcy, but sincerity alone will not change the past. You must show me the man you claim to be.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I understand your position, Elizabeth, and I shall strive to earn your trust and respect through my actions, not just my words.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will watch for your actions, Mr. Darcy, and hope that they prove your words true.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I will do all in my power to earn your regard, Elizabeth. Until then, I shall await the chance to prove myself.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I shall observe your actions closely, Mr. Darcy, and form my opinion accordingly.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your observation, Elizabeth, is a challenge I accept with the utmost seriousness. My conduct shall reflect the sincerity of my intentions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I believe you, Mr. Darcy, but actions will indeed speak louder than words. Let us leave it at that for now.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I shall endeavor to live up to your expectations, Elizabeth. May my actions indeed be a testament to my words.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
